answer: Yes. Use the `call-home` command in Operational Mode: `call-home [dial-out-server-name=]<string>`. It executes a manual connection trigger to a configured dial-out-server, forcing an immediate connection attempt. If the dial-out-server is currently in the 'connecting' state, the command forces an immediate attempt and will not wait for the retry interval before trying again. The pre-condition is that the dial-out server must already be configured for the command to execute properly. The dial-out-server-name parameter is the pre-configured name of the dial-out server (string, no default). Examples: `call-home collector-x`, `call-home dialoutservername`, and `call-home -h` for help. Note `auto-connect false` on a dial-out-server still allows manual connection via the call-home RPC.

Use `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>` (Operational or Candidate Configuration mode) to list configured telemetry subscriptions with encoding and transfer-mode. The `encoding` attribute specifies the data encoding scheme for data sent to and from the target device, and may be specified for all data or per-RPC if the target supports it; permitted values are json, bytes, proto, ascii and json-ietf, default json-ietf. The `transfer-mode` attribute specifies the data transfer mode to the target device: stream (values streamed by the target), once (values sent once-off by the target), or poll (values sent in response to a poll request), default stream. Related attributes include session-protocol (gnmi, default gnmi), session-type (gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel, gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc) and updates-only (true/false, default false).

No, YANG data models are not all loaded by default. The `data-model` object has an `enabled` attribute whose default is false; setting it true loads the model so it can be used via the management interfaces, and setting it false unloads it. Turn one on with `set data-model-<name> enabled true`, where name is the model name (String, length 0..256). Inspect models with `show data-model-<name> [description] [enabled]`, or just `show data-model` to view all available YANG data models for loading/unloading. `description` (String, length 0..256) is a show-only attribute. The command is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A dial-out-server's `retry-policy` is the retry policy applied after a timeout, with values progressive-back-off, retry-then-stop and retry-forever; the default is progressive-back-off. `retry` is the number of retries and is only applicable when retry-policy is retry-then-stop: Integer range 0..5, default 3. `timeout` is the time before the next retry, Integer range 1..255 seconds, default 10, and is not applicable for progressive-back-off (which has a dynamic timeout). The session `port` defaults to 4334, the default for the netconf protocol over ssh, and is configurable in the range 1..65535. `protocol` is netconf or restconf (default netconf) and transport is ssh. Example: `set dial-out-server-callhome1 auto-connect false retry-policy retry-then-stop port 4889 timeout 200 retry 5`.

Yes, gRPC/gNMI is enabled by default. The `grpc` object's `enabled` attribute enables or disables the gRPC management protocol and defaults to true. The `port` attribute is the port which listens for gNMI access via gRPC where gRPC is enabled, and defaults to 50051. Also configurable is `gnmi-get-encoding-granularity`, which controls the granularity of data in gNMI Get responses when encoded with JSON: per-path puts all path data in one Update message, per-object divides the path data into multiple Update messages, one per YANG container/list entry; the default is per-object. Use `show grpc [enabled] [port] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity]` and `set grpc enabled false` / `set grpc enabled true`. The object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted.

NETCONF listens on `port` for access via ssh, a port-number (uint16, range 1..65535) with default 830. The `hello-timeout` attribute specifies the number of seconds that a session may exist before the hello PDU is received/transmitted; the session is dropped if no hello PDU is received/transmitted before that many seconds elapse. It is a uint16 in the range 1..3600 seconds with a default of 2. Configure with `set netconf [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [hello-timeout <value>] [annotate-cli-name <value>] [static-info-in-notifs <value>]` and view with `show netconf`. NETCONF `enabled` defaults to true, and it is not possible to disable NETCONF from within a NETCONF session.

RESTCONF itself is enabled by default (`enabled` true), but plain HTTP is not: `http-enabled` defaults to false, and RESTCONF HTTP access is not supported in secure mode. `https-enabled` defaults to true. Ports are `http-port` default 8080 and `https-port` default 8181, both in range 1..65535. Session lifetime is controlled by `cookie-timeout`, the timeout of a cookie based RESTCONF session, in the range 1..300 minutes with a default of 5; the cookie expiration date is reset every time there is activity on the session. Example: `set restconf cookie-timeout 10`. `show restconf` also displays the read-only `api-root` (root of the RESTCONF API, String length 0..64).

Use `show snmp [enabled] [port] [snmp-engine-id] [engine-boot-count]`. The `snmp-engine-id` is a show-only attribute giving the SNMP EngineID of the NE; it follows EngineID format 3 as defined in RFC3411, and the MAC address in the Engine ID is the first MAC address of the NE's MAC address pool (String, length 0..256). `engine-boot-count` is also show-only and counts how many times the engine has restarted (Number, uint16, default 0). The settable attributes are `enabled` (true/false, default true, global SNMP access) and `port`, the port on which the NE listens for SNMP requests (range 1..65535, default 161). Note the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object, not here.

No. The `community-string-access` attribute of snmp-community defines the SNMP access right of the community string, and read-only is the only permitted value as well as the default. Create a community with `add snmp-community-<name> community-string <value> [enabled <value>] [community-string-access <value>]`, where `name` is the community name, distinct from the community string itself (String, length 0..64), `community-string` is the string itself (String, length 1..32, mandatory), and `enabled` turns the community-string on or off (true/false, default true). Example: `add snmp-community-mycommunity community-string public community-string-access read-only enabled true`. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The trap-community-string lives in the snmp-target object.

Add a trap listener with `add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>]`. `target-name` is String 0..32. `snmp-version` may be v2c or v3, default v2c. `trap-community-string` is the community string used for SNMP traps, String 0..32, default infinera. `target-port` is the UDP port number, range 0..65535, default 162, and `target-transport` is udp (only value, default udp). `snmpv3-user` applies only when snmp-version is v3. `enabled` defaults to true. `target-address` is the IPv4/IPv6 address or hostname of the target, optionally with a %zone index.

A new SNMPv3 user gets `user-sec-level` no-auth-no-priv by default; the permitted values are auth-no-priv, auth-priv and no-auth-no-priv. The privacy protocol `priv-protocol` may be DES, AES128, AES192 or AES256, with AES128 as the default. Authentication protocol `auth-protocol` supports only SHA (default SHA). Create with `add snmpv3-user-<snmpv3-user-name> auth-passphrase <value> priv-passphrase <value> [user-sec-level <value>] [auth-protocol <value>] [priv-protocol <value>]`; the user name is String length 1..32 and both passphrases are String length 8..64. Example: `add snmpv3-user-bob user-sec-level auth-priv auth-protocol SHA auth-passphrase public123 priv-protocol AES128 priv-passphrase private123`.

The `subscription-path-mode` attribute of subscription-path controls how subscription updates are sent: target-defined, on-change, or sample; the default is target-defined. View with `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name> [subscription-path] [subscription-path-origin] [subscription-path-mode] [sample-interval] [heartbeat-interval] [suppress-redundant]`. `sample-interval` is the time in milliseconds between samples of a telemetry data source (default 0, meaning optional); for a target-defined stream subscription with sample-interval unset, the system automatically adjusts it from 0 to 10 seconds. `heartbeat-interval` (milliseconds, default 0) is the maximum interval between updates; for a target-defined stream subscription with sample-interval unset and heartbeat-interval below 10 seconds, the system adjusts it to 20 seconds. `suppress-redundant` (true/false, default true) suppresses redundant updates.

Use `show subscriptions`. That is the entire syntax; the command takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. It shows a list of subscriptions on the node. For the detail of telemetry subscriptions configured in the system, use `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>`, which exposes related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type, session-protocol, encoding, transfer-mode, updates-only and user-access. For the per-path detail of a subscription, use `show subscription-path` or `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>`, which exposes subscription-path, subscription-path-origin, subscription-path-mode, sample-interval, heartbeat-interval and suppress-redundant.

Telemetry is configured through the `telemetry` object, which is used to configure persistent and dynamic telemetry. The syntax is `show telemetry` and `set telemetry id <string>`, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The object has a single parameter, `id`, described as persistent and dynamic telemetry, of type string with length 0..4096 and no default. The telemetry object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: `show telemetry` displays the telemetry subscription. Beyond that single `id` attribute, no further distinction between persistent and dynamic telemetry is stated; the associated subscriptions are viewed with `show subscriptions`, `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>` and `show subscription-path`.

Use `show third-party-app-<app-name> [version] [vendor] [product] [label] [state] [information] [enable]`, or `show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> [version] [state] [information]`. The `state` attribute reports the third party app state with values running, stopped or failed, and its default is stopped. The `enable` attribute is the third-party-app enabled state: if enabled the app is started, and it is also enabled upon system restart; if disabled the app is stopped. Its values are true and false, and the default is false, so an app is not enabled by default. Other attributes are version (string 0..64), vendor (string 0..64), product (string 0..256) and information (string 0..1024). Set them with `set third-party-app-<app-name> ...` in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `add <tab>` to visualize all entity types that are creatable at that time. The `add` command creates a new managed entity in the system database; the entity id format varies by managed entity type. Some entities have mandatory attributes that must be provided at creation, and if a mandatory attribute is not provided in the command itself the CLI automatically asks for it. Non-mandatory attributes can also be initialized by supplying attribute-value pairs. Syntax: `add [-v|-m|-f] <entity id> [(<attribute> <value>) ...]`, with -v validating the command only (nothing created, replies 'OK' if valid), -m merging (best effort add: create if absent, update if present), -f forcing without confirmation, and -h for help. Entities managed by the system cannot be created with `add`. The guide lists the creatable entities (aaa-server, acl, card, dial-out-server, interface, snmp-target, tom, user, xcon and many more), each cross-referenced to its own command page.

Yes, by default. The `clear` command clears entries for the specified entity, and in all cases requires a user confirmation; a confirmation prompt is displayed if the -f flag is not provided. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation, and -h displays help. Syntax is `clear [-f] <subcommand> ...` and the command runs in Operational Mode. The subcommands are alarm, app, certificate, crl, database, file, isk, log, ospf, pm, recover-mode, system, topology, dns, statistics. Note that `clear system factory-reset` with the `shutdown` option is not supported on the L0 cards.

Yes, via the `show-alarm-columns` attribute of the `cli` object, which defines the columns to display in the output of the 'show alarm' CLI command. Permitted values are a list of columns separated by a comma, `default-columns` to show the pre-defined columns, or `default-columns,<additional-details>` to show that additional column alongside the pre-defined ones. The default is default-columns. This configuration has a global effect and takes effect on all CLI sessions. Examples: `set cli show-alarm-columns col1,col2,col3` and `set cli show-alarm-columns default-columns,corrective-action`. Other cli attributes are enabled (true/false, default true; CLI cannot be disabled from within a CLI session), port for CLI access via ssh (range 1..65535, default 22), read-only script-dir (String 1..80), and default-interactive-mode (true/false, default true).

Use `set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value>`. The `cli-lines` attribute is the configurable number of rows used for display before pausing the output; after pausing, pressing [SPACEBAR] resumes display. Its range is 10..1000 with a default of 40. Width is set with `cli-columns`, the configurable number of columns used for display, range 80..4000, default 80. View with `show cli-session-config-<session-id> [cli-lines] [cli-columns] [interactive-mode] [display-timestamp]`. Examples: `set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-lines 30` and `set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-columns 100`. Also per-session are interactive-mode (true/false, default true, not persistent) and display-timestamp (true/false, default false).

Yes. The `connect` command establishes an ssh session directly from the CLI. Syntax: `connect [target-address=]<value> [user-name=]<value> [[port=]<value>]`, available in Operational Mode. `target-address` may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or hostname if DNS is configured; it requires connectivity and is a mandatory attribute. `user-name` is a string of 0..64 characters. `port` is optional; by default port 22 is used, but another may be provided if needed, which is useful to access the shell port. Example: `connect 10.41.24.55 admin port=8022`, which then adds the host to the known hosts list and prompts for the remote user's password.

Yes, use the `convert` command: `convert [target-representation=]<value> [command=]<value>`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. target-representation values are netconf-xml (an entire NETCONF xml payload), netconf-python (Python code performing a NETCONF request), restconf-json (HTTP method, URI, headers and body with JSON payloads), restconf-xml (same with XML payloads), restconf-python, plaintext-to-encrypted (encrypts a string using security-policies/csp-passphrase), snmp-oids (OIDs for objects in a 'show' command) and netsnmp-cmd (a shell command performing the SNMP request). The command should be enclosed in quotes; multiple CLI commands separated by ';' are merged into one payload where possible. Generated Python works with Python 2 or 3 and needs ncclient for NETCONF or requests for RESTCONF; host, IP and user-name are auto-filled, only the password must be entered. Example: `convert restconf-python 'ping 1.23.151.23'`.

No. The `default` command assigns default values to the targeted entities, which is useful to reset an entity after changes, but some configuration attributes will not be reset to default, including mandatory parameters and attributes that are only settable at creation. Syntax: `default [-f] [entity-id=][,]* [[attribute=][,]*]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. If attributes are specified, only those are set to their default value; otherwise all possible configuration attributes are defaulted. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation and -h shows help. Multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard (*). Examples: `default user-peter`, `default alarm-severity-entry-FAN/*`, `default alarm-severity-entry-*`, and `default tom-1-4-T16 label,phy-mode`. The default command is not supported in 1830 GX G30 Releases 5.0 and 5.1.

Use the -b flag: `delete -b <object>` is the best effort delete introduced in R9.0. It only bypasses the check for object existence without returning a failure, so it does not fail if the object does not exist, whereas standard `delete <object>` does fail in that case. It has the same functionality as a NETCONF 'remove' operation. Caveat: -b does not raise an error if the object is missing, but it may still produce other errors such as precondition failures. Syntax is `delete [-f|-v|-b] <entity-id> [<filter> ...]`. In a script you will normally combine it with -f, which forces the command without confirmation, since delete otherwise displays a confirmation prompt. -v validates only, executing no deletion and replying 'OK' if valid. Deleting an entity also removes all its sub-level objects, and is rejected if the entity or its sub-level containers carry services or other traffic affecting configuration.

The `exit` command logs you out of the current CLI mode: it terminates the current CLI session if you are in operational mode, or leaves configuration mode if you are in candidate mode. A confirmation prompt is displayed unless the -f flag is provided. Syntax: `exit [-h|-f]`, where -f forces the command without confirmation and -h displays help; access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The keyboard shortcut Ctrl+D has the same effect as `exit -f`, that is, it exits immediately without the confirmation prompt. Example: `exit -f`.

Use the `expect` command, which ensures an attribute matches an expected value: `expect [-r] [<instance>=]<value> [<expected-value>=]<value> [<attribute>=]<value>`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. If the value matches, no output is seen; if it does not, an ERROR message is shown. It is intended for scripts and automation to guarantee specific assumptions, and can be invoked multiple times to validate multiple attributes. Wildcards to select multiple object instances or attributes are not supported. If the script runs in 'stop-on-error' mode, a failed expect stops the script immediately. The -r flag enables regex mode, making the expected-value a regular expression instead of a literal string. Examples: `expect ne ne-name GX-NE-123` and `expect -r software-load-active swload-version R5.*`.
